extracted.intended_audience: general public and media professionals interested in journalism and media-ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implicit criteria around verifying reporting, distinguishing journalism from theatre, and handling errors — drawn from a news article about This American Life's retraction of a reported piece. Focus is on practices newsrooms should follow to ensure accuracy and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to journalistic standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Our program adheres to the same journalistic standards as the other national shows, and in this case, we did not live up to those standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad expectation that pieces broadcast as journalism meet established newsroom standards for accuracy and verification. If a program presents material as journalism, it must be treated with the same verification rigor as other national news shows; failure to do so is a serious lapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-check all substantive claims, including seemingly small details
rubrics_metrics.description: Some of the falsehoods found in Daisey's monologue are small ones: the number of factories Daisey visited in China, for instance, and the number of workers he spoke with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should verify not only dramatic or headline-grabbing claims but also granular details (counts, locations, timelines). Small factual inaccuracies can undermine credibility and indicate larger fabrication. Use independent confirmation whenever possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify key facts about incidents (location, participants, causation)
rubrics_metrics.description: In his monologue he claims to have met a group of workers who were poisoned on an iPhone assembly line by a chemical called n-hexane. Apple's audits of its suppliers show that an incident like this occurred in a factory in China, but the factory wasn't located in Shenzhen, where Daisey visited. 'It happened nearly a thousand miles away, in a city called Suzhou.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting on incidents (e.g., poisonings, underage labor), confirm the exact location, timing, and actors. Misplacing an incident geographically or attributing encounters to trips that did not happen is a substantive error; corroborate with documents, audits, or direct interviews with those affected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify identity and contact information of sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Glass says Daisey lied to him and his producer about the name of his interpreter and he also said the cell phone number he had for her didn't work anymore and he had no way to get back in touch with her.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsrooms should confirm the identities and reliable contact means of key sources before relying on them. If a source's identity or contact cannot be confirmed, treat the information as unverified and seek additional corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely solely on a single unverified source; pursue independent corroboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Marketplace tracked down Daisey's interpreter, who disputed parts of Daisey's monologue... In Schmitz's report, he confronts Daisey and Daisey admits to fabricating these characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent reporting (e.g., reaching primary sources directly, interviewing interpreters or affected workers) is essential to validate claims relayed by a single storyteller. Confrontation and double-checking can reveal discrepancies or fabrications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate and label theatre versus journalism clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: 'I'm not going to say that I didn't take a few shortcuts in my passion to be heard,' Daisey tells Schmitz and Glass. 'My mistake, the mistake I truly regret, is that I had it on your show as journalism, and it's not journalism. It's theater.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When broadcasting or publishing material that is theatrical, staged, or a performance piece, outlets must clearly disclose its nature. Excerpting a one-person show as journalism without explicit labeling risks misleading audiences; avoid presenting theatrical storytelling as factual reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kill or withhold publication when key verification fails
rubrics_metrics.description: "At that point, we should've killed the story," said Glass in a statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If verification of a central source or claim fails and cannot be resolved, editorial judgment should favor not running the piece. Unresolved doubts about fundamental elements warrant withholding or killing a story until corroboration is obtained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroborate anecdotal claims with documentary evidence and audits
rubrics_metrics.description: Apple's audits of its suppliers show (PDF) the company has caught underage workers at a handful of its suppliers. These things are rare, but together, they form an easy-to-understand narrative about Apple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use available documentary records (company audits, reports, official documents) to corroborate anecdotal or testimonial claims. Even when documents support the general pattern, ensure the specific anecdotes being reported align with the documentary record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be transparent: issue corrections, retractions, and devote coverage to errors
rubrics_metrics.description: We'll append a note. Also, This American Life will devote a considerable amount of time on Sunday's show to this matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When errors are identified, outlets should append notes or corrections to the original piece, retract when necessary, and explain to audiences what went wrong and how. Public acknowledgement and follow-up coverage help restore accountability and trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the reputational and public-impact consequences of reporting errors
rubrics_metrics.description: The piece essentially made Daisey Apple's chief critic and it also inspired a Change.org petition that collected more than 250,000 signatures demanding that Apple better the working conditions at the factories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should weigh the potential public influence of a story — including activism and policy pressure that may follow — and thus apply heightened scrutiny to highly influential pieces. High-impact reporting warrants especially thorough verification.
